description: Updates arrive every night between ten in the evening and six in the morning, Vienna time, weekends included. A weekly window looked cheaper and was not: Renovate picks its own moment to look at a repository, and a look which landed outside the seven hours of a Monday morning cost that repository a whole week. Four of the five repositories reading this preset went untouched on the last such Monday while their dashboards filled up.
The window lives here rather than in each repository, and so does the time zone, because a repository which copies the first and forgets the second silently keeps the window in UTC.
Automerging keeps no window of its own. A pull request opened at three whose build turns green at seven is still merged, which is why 'automergeSchedule' is left at its default.

Five pull requests per hour. The runner budget belongs to the whole organisation, and a backlog of fifteen updates across five repositories would spend a night of it at once. Draining the queue over a few nights arrives at the same place for less. The default of two was never a decision, and it is what let one repository merge two updates in a week while the rest of its queue sat until the next Monday.

'minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour' is loosened because the strict default blocks silently. A release whose datasource reports no publication date can never become five days old, so Renovate parks it as pending and lists it on the dashboard under a heading which reads like a build is running. Every repository had 'actions/setup-java v6' stuck there. What tolerating a missing date costs is the waiting period for those releases, and that is the smaller loss.

packageRules.description: Group all Spring Boot and Spring Framework dependencies

A patch merges itself once the required checks passed. The builds of these repositories run their own tests against a real engine or cluster, so a green pipeline is a strong statement for a patch. What that statement does not cover is listed in the rules below, which come after this one and therefore win.
Tools and test libraries merge themselves for a minor as well: they never reach a released artifact, and a break shows up as a red build rather than as behaviour in production.
The workflows of the repository are covered by the run that uses them, so a minor and a digest merge themselves too.

A patch of Spring Boot or Quarkus is upkeep inside the line a repository already promises, so it merges itself like every other patch. It travels in a pull request of its own because the minor above it waits for a person, and a group is only as fast as the slowest thing in it.

A minor of Spring Boot or Quarkus is a promise: the README of each repository names the platform versions it is built against, and an application picks them itself. Moving the line is a decision about what is supported, so it is read and merged by a person even when the build is green. A major is covered by the last rule of this file.

A patch of the BPMS stays inside the line a build already requires, and the builds of these repositories run their tests against a real engine or cluster of that line, so it merges itself like every other patch. It is grouped apart from the minor next to it, which is not going to merge itself.

The same for Camunda 8. The Camunda 8 adapter maintains a pin per release line and takes those out of this group in its own configuration, so what is left here are the ordinary io.camunda dependencies of a repository.

A minor of the BPMS is never merged by a robot. The engine or the client a build was compiled against decides which server versions the artifact accepts, which is a statement about every application that consumes it, and a green build says nothing about the clusters nobody here runs. The Camunda 8 adapter refines this per release line in its own configuration. A major is covered by the last rule of this file.
A major is read by a person. It is the update where a green build proves the least, since nothing compiles differently until something behaves differently.
